lead: In a free metal ion, the five d orbitals have the same energy. When ligands come near, their electron clouds repel the metal d electrons unequally. Some d orbitals point straight at the ligands and rise in energy; others point between them and stay lower. This splitting is called crystal field splitting. The model that explains it, and the size of the gap, is crystal field theory. The pattern and size of the splitting depend on geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, square planar) and on how strong the ligand field is. It explains why complexes are coloured, why some are magnetic, and why d⁴ to d⁷ complexes choose high-spin or low-spin arrangements.
prereq: You need: 1.6 for complex formation, oxidation states and ligand naming.

sections.h3: Why the five d orbitals split

blocks.text: In a free metal ion, the five d orbitals — d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>, d<sub>x²−y²</sub> and d<sub>z²</sub> — have the same energy. They are degenerate. Ligands carry lone-pair electrons. When six ligands approach along the ±x, ±y and ±z axes in an octahedral complex, their electron clouds repel the metal d electrons. The repulsion is not equal for all five orbitals.

The d<sub>x²−y²</sub> and d<sub>z²</sub> orbitals point along the axes, straight at the ligands. They feel strong repulsion and rise in energy. The d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> orbitals lie between the axes. They feel less repulsion and stay lower. The energy gap between the two sets is Δ<sub>o</sub> (o for octahedral). The average energy of the five orbitals is the barycentre. Relative to it, the upper two orbitals rise by +0.6Δ<sub>o</sub> and the lower three fall by −0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>. The total shift is zero: 2(+0.6) + 3(−0.4) = 0. This keeps the barycentre fixed.

blocks.where: Δ<sub>o</sub> is the octahedral crystal field splitting energy; eg is the upper set (d<sub>x²−y²</sub>, d<sub>z²</sub>); t<sub>2g</sub> is the lower set (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>).

sections.h3: Octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar patterns

blocks.text: In an octahedral complex, the two upper orbitals are labelled eg and the three lower orbitals are labelled t<sub>2g</sub>. The size of Δ<sub>o</sub> depends on the metal ion and on the ligands. Strong-field ligands such as CN<sup>−</sup> and CO give a large Δ<sub>o</sub>. Weak-field ligands such as H<sub>2</sub>O and Cl<sup>−</sup> give a smaller Δ<sub>o</sub>.

In a tetrahedral complex, four ligands sit at alternate corners of a cube. No d orbital points directly at the ligands. The splitting is smaller and inverted. The lower set is e (d<sub>x²−y²</sub>, d<sub>z²</sub>) at −0.6Δ<sub>t</sub> and the upper set is t<sub>2</sub> (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>) at +0.4Δ<sub>t</sub>. The relation is Δ<sub>t</sub> = (4/9)Δ<sub>o</sub>. Fewer ligands and no direct overlap make Δ<sub>t</sub> much smaller than Δ<sub>o</sub>.

A square planar complex is an extreme distortion of octahedral geometry with the two axial ligands removed. It is common for d⁸ ions such as Pt(II) and Pd(II). The d<sub>x²−y²</sub> orbital points directly at the four ligands and is raised most. The other orbitals lie lower, roughly in the order d<sub>xy</sub> > d<sub>z²</sub> > d<sub>xz</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>, with d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> degenerate and lowest. Splitting is large, so square planar complexes are usually low spin.

Crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE) is the net energy change when d electrons occupy the split orbitals, measured from the barycentre. A negative CFSE means the complex is stabilised. For octahedral complexes, count electrons in t<sub>2g</sub> (n<sub>t2g</sub>) and in eg (n<sub>eg</sub>). Use the formula below. Pairing energy P is the repulsion cost of putting two electrons in one orbital.
CFSE<sub>oct</sub> = (−0.4 n<sub>t2g</sub> + 0.6 n<sub>eg</sub>)Δ<sub>o</sub>;  CFSE<sub>tet</sub> = (−0.6 n<sub>e</sub> + 0.4 n<sub>t2</sub>)Δ<sub>t</sub>
blocks.where: n<sub>t2g</sub>, n<sub>eg</sub>, n<sub>e</sub>, n<sub>t2</sub> are the numbers of electrons in those orbital sets; Δ<sub>o</sub> and Δ<sub>t</sub> are the splitting energies in the two geometries.

blocks.text: For d⁴ to d⁷ ions in an octahedral field, two arrangements compete. If Δ<sub>o</sub> < P, electrons spread out over all five orbitals: high spin. If Δ<sub>o</sub> > P, electrons pair in the lower t<sub>2g</sub> set: low spin. Take d⁴. High spin is t<sub>2g</sub>³ eg¹, CFSE = −1.2Δ<sub>o</sub> + 0.6Δ<sub>o</sub> = −0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>. Low spin is t<sub>2g</sub>⁴, CFSE = −1.6Δ<sub>o</sub> + P. Low spin wins when −1.6Δ<sub>o</sub> + P < −0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>, that is Δ<sub>o</sub> > P. Ions d¹ to d³ and d⁸ to d¹⁰ have no such choice.

Tetrahedral Δt is only about 4/9 of Δo. It is usually smaller than the pairing energy, so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high spin. Colour and magnetic moments follow from these splittings; they are covered in 1.8.

figure.caption: The same five d orbitals split differently in three geometries. In an octahedral field the two eg orbitals rise by +0.6Δo and the three t2g orbitals fall by −0.4Δo; the tetrahedral pattern is inverted and smaller, and square planar raises dx²−y² most.

spec.aria: A tree splits the five d orbitals by geometry: octahedral gives eg above t2g, tetrahedral gives e below t2, and square planar raises dx²−y² most.

examples.question: Find the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE) of the complex ion [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>. The ligand H<sub>2</sub>O is weak-field. Use Δ<sub>o</sub> for the octahedral splitting.
steps: Let the oxidation state of Cr be x. The complex has charge +3 and six neutral H<sub>2</sub>O ligands: x + 6(0) = +3, so x = +3.
Cr has atomic number 24. Cr<sup>3+</sup> has 24 − 3 = 21 electrons. The argon core holds 18 electrons. The remaining d electrons are 21 − 18 = 3. Configuration is d³.
Six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands give octahedral geometry. The d orbitals split into t<sub>2g</sub> (lower) and eg (upper).
For d³, the three electrons fill the lower t<sub>2g</sub> set singly: t<sub>2g</sub>³ eg⁰. No electron pairing is needed, so the pairing energy does not enter.
examples.answer: CFSE = −1.2Δ<sub>o</sub>; the negative sign means the d³ configuration is stabilised by 1.2Δ<sub>o</sub>.

traps: Do not treat Δ<sub>t</sub> as equal to Δ<sub>o</sub>. Tetrahedral splitting is Δ<sub>t</sub> = (4/9)Δ<sub>o</sub>, much smaller, so most tetrahedral complexes are high spin.
Do not swap the labels. In octahedral fields eg is higher and t<sub>2g</sub> is lower. In tetrahedral fields e is lower and t<sub>2</sub> is higher.
CFSE is negative when the complex is stabilised. A positive CFSE means destabilisation. Pairing energy P must be added when electrons are forced to pair in one orbital.
Square planar is not the same as octahedral. The d<sub>x²−y²</sub> orbital is strongly raised in square planar complexes such as Pt(II) and Pd(II).
High-spin and low-spin choices exist only for d⁴ to d⁷ in octahedral fields. d¹ to d³ and d⁸ to d¹⁰ have only one filling pattern.

quiz.q: Name the two d-orbital sets in an octahedral complex and say which is higher in energy.
quiz.a: The lower set is t<sub>2g</sub> (d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub>, d<sub>yz</sub>). The higher set is eg (d<sub>x²−y²</sub>, d<sub>z²</sub>).

quiz.q: Why is the t<sub>2g</sub> set lower than eg in an octahedral field?
quiz.a: The six ligands lie on the axes. The eg orbitals point along the axes, straight at the ligands, so their electrons feel strong repulsion and rise in energy. The t<sub>2g</sub> orbitals point between the axes, feel less repulsion and stay lower.

quiz.q: Calculate the CFSE of an octahedral d² complex. No pairing occurs. Give the answer in terms of Δ<sub>o</sub>.
For an octahedral d⁴ complex, derive the condition for low-spin behaviour using CFSE and pairing energy P.
quiz.a: High spin: t<sub>2g</sub>³ eg¹, CFSE = 3(−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>) + 1(0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>) = −0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>. Low spin: t<sub>2g</sub>⁴, CFSE = 4(−0.4Δ<sub>o</sub>) + P = −1.6Δ<sub>o</sub> + P. Low spin is favoured when −1.6Δ<sub>o</sub> + P < −0.6Δ<sub>o</sub>, which simplifies to Δ<sub>o</sub> > P.

quiz.q: Write the relation between tetrahedral splitting Δ<sub>t</sub> and octahedral splitting Δ<sub>o</sub> for the same metal and ligands.
quiz.a: Δ<sub>t</sub> = (4/9)Δ<sub>o</sub>, so tetrahedral splitting is smaller.

quiz.q: Find the CFSE of a tetrahedral high-spin d⁵ complex in terms of Δ<sub>t</sub>.
quiz.a: Tetrahedral high-spin d⁵: e² t<sub>2</sub>³. CFSE = 2(−0.6Δ<sub>t</sub>) + 3(+0.4Δ<sub>t</sub>) = −1.2Δ<sub>t</sub> + 1.2Δ<sub>t</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: Why are tetrahedral complexes usually high spin, even when the metal has a d⁴ to d⁷ configuration?
quiz.a: Tetrahedral splitting Δ<sub>t</sub> is only 4/9 of Δ<sub>o</sub> and is usually smaller than the pairing energy P. Electrons then avoid pairing and occupy the upper t<sub>2</sub> set, giving a high-spin arrangement.

beyond: Not for the exam. Crystal field theory is the electrostatic first approximation; ligand field theory adds covalent mixing between metal and ligand orbitals and explains why CO and CN<sup>−</sup> produce large splitting. The spectrochemical series orders ligands by Δ<sub>o</sub>. These ideas guide the design of catalysts, MRI contrast agents and magnetic materials. Search 'spectrochemical series', 'ligand field theory' and 'Jahn-Teller distortion' to go further.
